newsitem.title: UK: Sterling/mark lifted in Europe by German gold rift.
newsitem.headline: Sterling/mark lifted in Europe by German gold rift.

text.p: Sterling was lifted in morning Europe against the mark, up over a pfennig on concerns that EMU might not go ahead on time after the Bundesbank on Wednesday renounced German government plans to revalue its assets.
Sterling/mark was up to 2.7840/50 by 0815 GMT compared to 2.7720/30 in late Europe on Wednesday.
"The market seems to have interpreted last night's comments as increasing the chances of an EMU delay," said Nicholas Stamenkovic, an economist at DKB international here.
"All European bonds markets are being sold. People are wary of uncertainty and are just looking for temporary safe havens."
Analysts cited sterling along with the dollar and the Swiss franc as safe havens from the weaker mark.
Any rise in sterling/mark would, however, be muted as Britain's chances of participating in EMU were perceived to have increased since the Labour government was elected on May 1.

"People tend to use sterling in this light, but it is less applicable with a Labour government than sterling with a euro-sceptic government," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "But EMU' credibility has been tarnished."

Though the German government has said it will press ahead with the revaluation, it must still pass the reforms through parliament where it faces opposition from the Liberal Party. It must also be granted approval by Eurostat, the European Commission's accounting arm.
"There is still some lingering uncertainty over what is going to happen to EMU," said Stamenkovic. "Sterling will benefit as long as the uncertainty persists."
Sterling was buoyed by better than expected data showing the UK's April non-EU deficit at 335 million stg versus the forecast 600 million.
The UK March EU trade deficit was 20 million stg, with a global shortfall of 671 million.
The UK EU-harmonised CPI index rose by 1.6 percent in the year to April, after a 1.8 percent year-on-year rise in March.
